passages.where: God tells Israel not to fear, and gives his reasons: he created them, redeemed them, called them by name, and will be with them through water and fire. The site's note on the chapter lists those reasons in that order. The promise is not that there will be no rivers to cross, but that they will not cross them alone.

David asks whom he shall fear, with the LORD as his light, salvation and stronghold. The site's plain note says the question is asked because there is something to fear, and that the same man prays in anguish later in the psalm. Courage in the Bible, it says, is not the absence of fear; it is trust that holds when fear is present.

After Abram has defeated four kings, made enemies in the east and refused Sodom's wealth, God tells him not to be afraid: I am your shield, your very great reward. The site's note says God speaks to both fears, protection and provision. The plain note adds that when Abram brought God his honest worry, God did not scold him but took him outside to see the stars.

Trapped between Pharaoh's chariots and the sea, the people panic, and Moses tells them not to be afraid but to stand firm and see the LORD's salvation; the LORD will fight for them. The site's note on the chapter tells how the sea was divided and they crossed on dry ground. Fear here is answered not by a plan but by a promise, and the people are asked to be still before they are asked to walk.

The shepherd's psalm walks through the valley of the shadow of death and fears no evil, for you are with me. The site's plain note says the promise is not that the sheep will never be in danger, but that the shepherd will never leave, and that the comfort of verse 4 is not you will not go into the valley but you are with me in it.

David says he sought the LORD, who answered him and delivered him from all his fears. The site's plain note points out where he learned it: not in a palace, but pretending to be mad in an enemy city. Deliverance from fear came to a frightened man in a humiliating place.

Sending his disciples out to face rejection, Jesus tells them not to fear, because sparrows, the cheapest food in the market, do not fall apart from their Father, and the hairs of their head are numbered. The site's note says the argument moves from the least to the greater. The plain note asks the reader to name something they are afraid of and put it beside the sparrow.

The disciples are straining at the oars against the wind in the night, and when they see Jesus walking on the sea they cry out in terror. He speaks at once: take courage, it is I, do not be afraid. The site's note says the words of comfort are also words of revelation, and the plain note says that Jesus saw them straining while he was far away on the mountain, though they did not know he saw.

In Gethsemane Jesus is deeply troubled and distressed, says his soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death, and prays that the cup be taken from him, yet not what I will. The site's plain note says he felt horror at death as a real man would, and freely gave his will to the Father's. Fear is not sin; Jesus himself was afraid, and he said so to his friends and to his Father.

On Patmos John sees the glorified Son of Man and falls at his feet like a dead man. The risen Christ places his right hand on him and says do not be afraid: he was dead and is alive forever, and he holds the keys of Death and of Hades. In the Bible's last book the risen Christ says to a terrified man what the angel said to the shepherds at his birth (Luke 2:10): do not be afraid.

misread.taken: God has not given us a spirit of fear is used to tell anxious or frightened Christians that their fear proves weak faith, or that it does not come from God and so should simply stop.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul is speaking to Timothy about courage in his work, not shrinking back from the gospel or from a friend in chains. He is not saying that anyone who feels fear has a weak faith; Paul himself admits to sorrow and to being anxious. The verse points a fearful person to what God gives and does not shame them for being afraid, and it is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in the verse forbids it.

whole: Fear comes in many sizes. A scan result not yet back. A child out late with the roads icy. A court date, a layoff rumor, a lump, a letter from the bank. Some fears are sudden and sharp; others have been living in the chest so long they feel like part of the furniture. Christians often carry an extra weight on top of the fear itself: the sense that a person with real faith would not be afraid, so the fear must also be a spiritual failure. They pray, and the fear does not leave, and they conclude something is wrong with them. If fear has become constant, wakes you at night, or brings panic you cannot stop, it is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.

Scripture says do not be afraid again and again, and it says it to people in real danger. It says it to Abram after a battle, to a people trapped against the sea, to disciples straining at the oars in the dark, to John lying at the feet of the risen Christ. The Bible does not treat fear as shameful. David asks whom he shall fear and then prays in anguish a few verses later. Jesus in Gethsemane was deeply distressed and said so. The real danger the Bible names is not feeling afraid but letting fear decide: hiding what God has given, refusing what he asks, or trusting only what we can control. Most of us know that pull. We plan, check and rehearse, and the fear grows because we have made ourselves the only one standing between us and the thing we dread.

So the Bible's wisdom answers fear not with a technique but with a person. Do not fear, God says, and almost always gives a reason: I have redeemed you, I am your shield, I am with you, it is I. When you are afraid, David says, put your trust in God; the fear comes first, and trust is what you do with it. Tell God plainly what you are afraid of, as Jesus did in the garden, and tell someone near you too. Ask for what you need and leave room for the Father's will. Remember what God has already done, the way Israel remembered the sea. And take the next step that is yours to take, even shaking; courage in Scripture is trust that holds while the fear is still there.

The hope Scripture gives is that the one who says do not be afraid has gone through the worst thing himself. Jesus was afraid in Gethsemane, went to the cross, and rose, and now he holds the keys of Death and of Hades. The shepherd does not promise there will be no valley; he promises to be in it. Not one sparrow falls apart from your Father, and you are worth more than many sparrows. Fear may still come tomorrow. It does not get the last word.
sit: What are you most afraid of right now, and what would it change to say it out loud to God, and to one person you trust, this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer of someone hounded and afraid. The site's plain note says verse 3 does not say I am never afraid; it says when I am afraid. Fear comes. Trust is what you do with it.
